findings.problem: Open point settled: the claim is accurate (the Seven Years' War roughly doubled Britain's national debt, and the Stamp Act of 1765 was meant to help pay for troops kept in America), but the cited Seven Years' War article says nothing of the debt or the Stamp Act, so a student following the ref cannot check the sentence. The ref should be replaced or supplemented (for example with the Stamp Act 1765 article); the text needs no change.

Viscardo did not publish the letter: he died in London in 1798 and Francisco de Miranda published it in 1799. The sourceLine says only 'published 1799', so the note should not make Viscardo the publisher.

edit.old: Viscardo, a Peruvian-born Jesuit exile, wrote c. 1791 and published in 1799 to persuade Spanish Americans. He claims that only creoles should fill offices in their own country and attacks Spanish adventurers, so the letter shows the creole interest in office and wealth well before 1808, though an exile's propaganda is not a measure of widespread opinion.

He claims that only creoles should fill offices in their own country and attacks Spanish adventurers, so the letter shows the creole interest in office and wealth well before 1808, though an exile's propaganda is not a measure of widespread opinion.

findings.problem: Haiti is usually counted as part of Latin America, and the Haitian Revolution is taught beside the Latin American revolutions in 5.2, so saying the source 'is not about Latin America' is wrong and would wrongly tell a student that Haiti is outside the prompt. The note means Spanish America.

edit.old: Dessalines was a general of the Haitian revolution, and this 1804 address is part of the Haitian declaration of independence. It shows what a successful rising of enslaved people looked like, which is the example that slaveholding creoles in Spanish America feared, but the source is not about Latin America and the fear has to be inferred from outside knowledge.

findings.problem: Only one viceroyalty was created between the 1760s and the 1780s, the Río de la Plata in 1776 (New Granada dates from 1717 and 1739), so 'created new viceroyalties' in that period overstates it.

edit.old: The Bourbon Reforms of the 1760s to 1780s created new viceroyalties, raised taxes and promoted peninsulares to high office, so creole elites lost ground in their home colonies before any independence movement began.

findings.problem: The Bolívar excerpt in this pool (the Angostura address on creole identity and a hereditary senate) says nothing about office or trade, and the Venezuelan declaration complains of representation, not trade, so 'all complain about exclusion from office and trade' is not supported by the documents.

edit.old: Corroborate across groups: Viscardo, the Venezuelan declaration and Bolívar all complain about exclusion from office and trade, which supports the creole-interests argument, while Morelos and San Martín show liberal ideas changing policy, so taken together they point to a movement driven by interest that adopted ideas it could not fully control.

findings.problem: The pool's own note on the Tucumán declaration says it 'says little about equality among social groups', so citing it as a place where ideas of equality were put into a declaration contradicts the document; and 1808 was not a rebellion (Beaver shows crowds proclaiming Ferdinand VII).

edit.old: Qualify with a counter-argument: although fear of the poor held many creoles back, ideas of equality were not merely decoration, since Morelos, San Martín and the Tucumán congress put them into decrees and declarations, and the rebellion of 1808 was at first loyal to the king, so a lot of the radical language came later.

findings.problem: The separate condenser of the late 1760s and 1770s cut coal use, but Watt's engines of that time pumped water; only the rotary-motion engines of the 1780s could drive machinery and free mills from riversides, so the sentence credits the earlier engine with a later change.

edit.old: James Watt's improved steam engine of the late 1760s and 1770s used a separate condenser to burn much less coal than earlier engines, and it freed factories from dependence on rivers and water power.
edit.new: James Watt's improved steam engine of the late 1760s and 1770s used a separate condenser to burn much less coal than earlier engines, and, once adapted to rotary motion in the 1780s, it freed factories from dependence on rivers and water power.

findings.problem: The excerpt describes the domestic system before machinery and the inventions of the second half of the 18th century, which Engels (born 1820, in Manchester from 1842) did not witness, so calling it 'first-hand evidence' teaches students a wrong sourcing judgement.

edit.old: Engels was a German socialist and manager in his father's Manchester cotton firm who wrote this in 1845 as a critic of industrial capitalism. He dates the English revolution to the steam engine and cotton machinery and describes spinning and weaving moving out of the family home, which is first-hand evidence of technology and wage labour, though his political purpose coloured his picture of the earlier period.

He dates the English revolution to the steam engine and cotton machinery and describes spinning and weaving moving out of the family home, which is evidence of technology and wage labour from a man who knew the factory system at first hand, though he had not seen the earlier period and his political purpose coloured his picture of it.

findings.problem: Smith did not write 'before the factory age': Arkwright's water-powered mill at Cromford opened in 1771, five years before The Wealth of Nations, though factories were still few.

edit.old: Smith was a Scottish political economist who wrote in 1776, before the factory age, criticising joint-stock companies for foreign trade because directors manage other people's money. It shows that such companies existed and that economists doubted their efficiency, so it complicates the claim that company law drove industrialization.

findings.problem: Muhammad Ali avoided foreign loans; his programme was undone by the 1838 trade treaty and the 1840 intervention (as outsideEvidence.0 says), and Egypt's foreign debt came under his successors Said and Ismail. Naming 'Muhammad Ali's Egypt' as a case of state action that relied on foreign loans and produced debt is wrong.

edit.old: Governments were necessary but not sufficient: state action worked best where it built on existing strengths and kept control of finance, as in Japan, but where it relied on foreign loans, monopolies and forced labour, as in Muhammad Ali's Egypt and the Tanzimat Ottoman Empire, it produced debt and foreign control instead of lasting industry.

findings.problem: Mrs. Austin (Sarah Austin) was Lucie Duff Gordon's mother, not a friend; the Letters from Egypt are mostly to her mother and her husband. Audience is part of the sourcing judgement students are taught.

edit.old: Lucie Duff Gordon was an English traveller living in Upper Egypt for her health, writing to a friend in November 1862. She describes hundreds of men taken from their homes to work on the Suez Canal or the Pasha's palaces for a nominal piastre a day, which shows the human cost of state projects in Egypt, but she is a sympathetic outside observer whose letter was written privately and published in 1865.

findings.problem: The excerpt describes centralising the army in 1871 so that 'the security of the restored monarchy was assured'; it says nothing of foreign threat, arms production or industry, so calling it 'strong evidence that defence needs drove state action' in a prompt about industrialization overstates what the document shows.

edit.old: Yamagata was the Field-Marshal who designed Japan's conscript army, writing in 1908 about the reforms of 1871. He shows the new government disbanding clan troops and centring military power on the state, so he is strong evidence that defence needs drove state action, but as an insider telling his own success story he stresses the achievement more than the cost.

He shows the new government disbanding clan troops and centring military power on the state, which is evidence of military reform driving state action, but the passage concerns the security of the new regime at home and says nothing of factories or foreign threats, and as an insider telling his own success story he stresses the achievement more than the cost.

findings.problem: Mitsui was a merchant house from the 17th century and Mitsubishi was founded before the 1880s sales, so saying the zaibatsu 'grew from this' overstates; the sales of state enterprises helped them grow.

edit.old: After the Meiji Restoration of 1868 the government built model factories, and in the 1880s it sold many of them to private firms; family-controlled combines called zaibatsu, such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi, grew from this.

findings.problem: Three of the four 'limits' sources are British (Duff Gordon, Cromer and Lane), not two, and 'two ... such as' misleads a student counting perspectives.

edit.old: Qualify with a counter-argument: two of the sources on limits are by British observers and officials such as Cromer and Duff Gordon, who may exaggerate the failures of governments they criticised, while Midhat, writing the life of his reforming father, may flatter the Tanzimat.

findings.problem: Churches and employers could not make rules binding on whole industries; the pool's own note on Rerum Novarum says the Pope's 'authority was moral and not legal'. The examples the thesis gives (factory and mines acts, Bismarck's insurance laws) are all state laws.

edit.old: Reform from above was the most effective response in the short term because only governments, employers and churches could make rules binding on whole industries, as the factory and mines acts of Britain and Bismarck's insurance laws did, but these reforms came largely because workers and socialists created pressure.

findings.problem: The prompt asks for relative effectiveness, but no document records an outcome: the sourcing notes themselves say the petition, the Manifesto, Proudhon, Owen and the 1881 message show aims or promises and not results, and the testimonies predate the laws. A student can judge effectiveness only from outside evidence; one document on a result (for example a factory inspector's report after 1833, or a source on the 1880s German insurance laws in operation) would let the pool support the task.
'being beaten and woken by his parents' reads as if his parents beat him; in the testimony his parents woke him and he was beaten when he came late to the mill, so the note misreports the document.

edit.old: Matthew Crabtree was a 22-year-old blanket manufacturer who had worked in a textile mill from the age of eight, testifying to the Sadler Committee of the House of Commons in 1832. He describes fourteen-hour days and being beaten and woken by his parents, which shows child labour as a family matter, but he spoke to a committee looking for evidence of abuse.

findings.problem: A world market did exist in 1750 (the Atlantic system, the Indian Ocean and silver trades of Unit 4), as this item's own contextualization.1 says; claiming it 'had not existed' is wrong and contradicts the notes. The change was one of scale and speed.

edit.old: To a great extent: steam power, factories, railways and steamships raised output and cut the time of transport (a railway at twenty-five miles an hour, a canal that shortened the route from Europe to the Indian Ocean), while the telegraph and cables joined distant markets, so by 1900 grain, cotton, timber and rubber were produced for a world market that had not existed in 1750.

findings.problem: Weeks wrote from Monsembe on the Upper Congo, far from the Matadi–Léopoldville railway in the Lower Congo, and his own question is how the railway benefits 'the natives on the Upper Congo'; he could not witness its dividends, so 'eyewitness evidence of who gained from the railway' is a wrong sourcing judgement.

edit.old: J. H. Weeks, a British Baptist missionary on the Upper Congo, wrote this letter in 1903 to E. D. Morel, who quoted it in Red Rubber (1906) for his reform campaign, so the passage was chosen to make a case. It claims that the Congo railway paid large dividends to shareholders while the people paid taxes and kept roads clear for nothing, which is eyewitness evidence of who gained from the railway.

Morel, who quoted it in Red Rubber (1906) for his reform campaign, so the passage was chosen to make a case. findings.problem: Yung Wing's document is about steamships, not the railway or the telegraph, so citing him for China's adoption of 'the railway and the telegraph' misreads the pool.

edit.old: Explain similarity and difference: the same technologies, the railway and the telegraph, were adopted by Japan and China through state and joint-stock effort (Den, Yung Wing) but imposed in India and the Congo by colonial rulers (Naoroji, Weeks, Gandhi), so the effect depended on who controlled them.

findings.problem: Nasmyth's passage explains why employers wanted self-acting tools; it gives no measure of how far machines spread, so it is not 'good evidence for the scale of mechanization'.

edit.old: James Nasmyth was a Manchester machine-tool maker who recalled the 1830s in his 1883 autobiography, so he speaks as an employer and seller of machines. He shows machines valued for accuracy and regularity and as a way to be rid of unreliable hand labour, which is good evidence for the scale of mechanization but also for how factory owners saw workers.

findings.problem: The excerpt says only that limited liability had until lately been the Bank of England's monopoly and needed a charter or statute; it says nothing of how the change was made (the Companies Acts of 1856–62), so 'evidence for how a new legal form was introduced' claims more than the document shows.

edit.old: Walter Bagehot, an English banker and editor of The Economist, wrote Lombard Street (1873) as an insider describing the London money market. He notes that limited liability in banks had long been a monopoly of the Bank of England and that the law allowed it only by charter or statute, so he is good evidence for how a new legal form was introduced, though he writes only about England.

findings.problem: The pool's own note puts Rizal 'at a reformist stage' (he asks for more liberty under Spain and only warns of independence), so listing him among those who 'sought to leave an existing empire' is wrong; and the Mazzini and Fichte excerpts define the nation by God-given peoples and language, not by hostility to foreign domination, which only Garibaldi's text expresses.

edit.old: Explain similarity and difference: Mazzini, Garibaldi and Fichte all define the nation by a shared people and hostility to foreign domination, but the Italian and German movements built new states by joining many small ones while Tucumán, Rizal and Mitchel sought to leave an existing empire, so the same idea unified in one place and divided in another.

findings.problem: The Charter Oath is dated the 14th day of the 3rd month in the Japanese calendar, which the sourceLine gives as 6 April 1868 in the Western calendar; 'March 1868' in an English note reads as a Western date and is wrong.

edit.old: The Charter Oath was issued in the name of Emperor Meiji by the new government in March 1868. It calls on all people, high and low, to unite their minds in conducting the affairs of the state and to seek knowledge throughout the world, which shows a government building a national identity from a divided class society, but it is an official statement of intent and not proof that people took it up.

It calls on all people, high and low, to unite their minds in conducting the affairs of the state and to seek knowledge throughout the world, which shows a government building a national identity from a divided class society, but it is an official statement of intent and not proof that people took it up.

findings.problem: The prompt asks for the extent of change, but this thesis argues what drove the change and never states an extent, so a student copying it would not have a thesis that answers the task.

edit.old: The change was driven by campaigns and reform from below as well as from above: abolitionists, strikers and factory reformers pushed governments, while owners and states protected property by compensation and apprenticeship, so continuity and change shaped each other.
edit.new: Labor systems changed to a real but limited extent, through campaigns and reform from below as well as from above: abolitionists, strikers and factory reformers pushed governments, while owners and states protected property by compensation and apprenticeship, so continuity and change shaped each other.
